program: ODSP assets, continued: Directives 4.4 (transfers), 4.5 (vehicles), 4.7 (trusts), 4.8 (life insurance). Complements rules.json (4.1).

4.4.title: Transfer of assets for inadequate consideration

status: DRAFT: written by Claude from the directive text. Not yet reviewed by a human.

rules.quote: One year prior to the date of application, members of an applicant's benefit unit cannot assign, transfer or dissipate assets in order to qualify for ODSP. This may be increased to three years if there is reason to believe that a three-year period of review is appropriate.

Inadequate consideration will be assumed if the property was knowingly transferred for an amount that is at least 25% less than market value unless there is an acceptable explanation or an exceptional circumstance.

Where the transfer was clearly made for the purpose of qualifying for income support, the person will be deemed ineligible. The period of ineligibility will be determined by dividing the additional amount the person should have received for a fair market value ... by [monthly income support]. The 'net amount of inadequacy' is the fair market value ... minus the money received ... and minus the maximum allowable asset limit after taking into account current assets.
The reduction shall be no less than 5% nor more than 20% of the income support and shall continue until such time as the inadequacy has been compensated.

An applicant/recipient may use assets to pay off pre-existing, previously recorded debts which, if not paid, could result in legal action being taken against them. ... Disposition of assets under these types of situations should not be considered an inadequate disposition of assets under ODSP.
Under ODSP, there is no limit on the value of one motor vehicle per benefit unit. Any member of the benefit unit may own the vehicle.
The value of a second vehicle that is required by a dependant to work outside the home is exempt up to $15,000.

If the value of a second vehicle required by a dependant for work is more than $15,000, any loans or encumbrances against the vehicle should be deducted from its value. ... an additional deduction of $500 should be applied to reflect the depreciation. After deducting any loans and encumbrances, and taking into account the depreciation, any portion of the value of a vehicle required by a working dependant which is over the threshold level of $15,000 should be considered an asset.
The total value of any additional vehicle owned by a member of the benefit unit, whether or not that vehicle is required for work, is treated as an asset.
The wholesale value listed in the Redbook is the amount which should be used to determine value.
Where the asset amount attributed for the vehicle is above the asset limit (combined with the value of other assets the recipient may have), the recipient will have six months to sell the vehicle.
The total combined amount of a trust plus the cash surrender value of any life insurance policies owned by a member of the benefit unit must not exceed $100,000.

Only funds that are derived from an inheritance or the proceeds of a life insurance policy can benefit from the asset exemption if placed in trust. Funds from different sources would not qualify for this asset exemption.
To allow a reasonable period of time to put the money in trust, recipients may be given up to six months to establish the trust.
A true absolute discretionary trust is not considered an asset for ODSP purposes, therefore the capital value of such a trust can be in excess of $100,000.

Members of the benefit unit who receive an inheritance or are entitled to an inheritance cannot create or put that inheritance in an absolute discretionary trust in an attempt to have the trust not considered an asset.
These trusts are normally considered an asset if the trustee is able to encroach on the capital for the person's maintenance, otherwise they are not an asset.
The income exemptions apply provided that an annual report documenting all income and expense transactions relating to the trust is filed.

Payments from a trust used for any purpose up to a maximum of $10,000 for any twelve month period are exempt as income. ... Payments used for approved disability related items or services or education or training expenses incurred because of a disability; payments used to purchase a principal residence or an exempt vehicle; or that will be applied to the first and last month's rent necessary to secure accommodation.

The cash surrender value of life insurance policies up to $100,000 for members of the benefit unit are exempt from inclusion as assets. If the person also has a trust fund, the combined value of the cash surrender value of the life insurance policy and trust fund must not exceed the $100,000 limit. This does not apply to a 'Henson' type trust, which is without limit.
Life insurance policies which have no cash surrender value are exempt as assets.

If the cash surrender value of the insurance policy is greater than $100,000 and the amount over $100,000, combined with all other non-exempt assets, exceeds the asset limit for the benefit unit, there is no financial eligibility for ODSP.
Annuities, deferred annuities and segregated funds purchased from a life insurance company are treated in the same way as life insurance under ODSP.

a policy may have a $2,000 cash surrender value according to the policy schedule. Information from the insurance company, however, indicates that $500 was borrowed. As a result, the cash surrender value (and value of the asset) now is only $1,500.
a partial redemption of the cash surrender value of a life insurance policy to a maximum of $10,000 in a 12 month period per member of the benefit unit who has a policy, can be used for any purpose.

flags_for_human_review: DISAGREEMENT: Second vehicle. Directive 4.1 says a second vehicle is exempt 'provided that its net value is no more than $15,000' (all or nothing). Directive 4.5 says it is exempt 'up to $15,000' and only the excess over $15,000 (after loans and a $500 depreciation deduction) counts. The screener now follows 4.5, which is more detailed. Needs confirmation.
4.4 and 4.8 refer to 'ODP' / 'Definition and Treatment of Assets' in places where they appear to mean ODSP / Income. Typos in the source, harmless.
4.4's examples use a $40,000 limit and a made-up $1,000 monthly benefit; the real period depends on the benefit calculation (estimate.py).
Trusts are very fact-specific ('Legal Services Branch should be consulted'). The screener should treat any trust other than a simple inheritance trust under $100,000 as 'unclear, ask a caseworker'.
4.5 refers to the Canadian Redbook wholesale value, which is a paid reference. A user-facing tool can only ask the user for their best estimate.
4.4 reduction is 5% to 20% 'depending on factors', which is discretionary; the tool should only say a reduction may apply.
